tweets.text:
When I explained to a friend what Claude Code can do today, I used Clojure's persistent hash map and implemented them in Python. 

Adding a key while returning a complete copy of the (immutable) hash is extremely cheap: With 1 million entries it's about 3000x faster than in Python. The cost for it is that adding a key is O(log n) and not O(1). 

The numbers below are for 1 million keys. So when the access pattern is to make frequent, small changes to a dictionary, they can be the right thing to use.

It's a functional data structure (lock-free and immutable) implemented as a Hash-array mapped trie.

Once you get a hang of these lock-free data structures you get a bit addicted to them - they're so elegant. They're making it easy to implement transactional changes without locks, without wasting time and space for deep copies, and global locks. In my view they should be part of every developer's toolbox.

So I first had it implemented in Python, including a test suite of 23 tests, plus a performance test. 

Python is not the ideal shell for it - it would thrive in a multithreaded, GIL-free world - but I figured it would make for a great example.

Then I asked it to keep the interface but move the implementation to C++, with a Python binding. It was able to write the code and execute the result right away, found a few bugs and solved them by itself on the spot. My rusty C++ knowledge would have missed some of the C++17 contraptions. The test suite acted as the spec, and the perf results set the stage for the next step.

So we went through a few rounds of perf optimization, reducing the load on heap allocations and the Python GIL, implemented a lazy iterator, added some Pythonic interface functions that make it look more similar to a Python dictionary, and added a readme. I've had a look through the code only twice and didn't change a single line.

That was a fun 2 hours.

Join group chats with your friends and orchestrate an endless swarm of AI agents to accomplish anything.

Spent some of holiday break building a POC collaborative AI agent orchestration app. ~4 days of prompting 3+ Claude Code terminals running Opus 4.5.

* Native SwiftUI for blazing fast cross-platform performance- MacOS, iOS, iPadOS
* Backend: Elixir+Phoenix framework for realtime state sync via WebSockets + channels + presence (same stack as @supabase realtime). Oban for agent bg worker lifecycle.

Roadmap:
1. Agent + sub agent orchestration, similar to Claude Code skills + subagents. Top-level orchestration agent inspects requests and examines available tools + env to maximize context efficiency via specialized agents.
2. Open agent details to inspect sub agent thought threads via separate detail views
3. MCP server support via @composio 
4. P2P agent communication and collaboration via native Elixir Registry module
5. Human-in-the loop requests and blocking client side tools (e.g. local files/apps as context)

tweets.text:
📝非エンジニア向けに、Claude Codeの「CLAUDE .md」に設定しておくと幸せになれるプロンプトが海外で話題

✅️設定する内容
 - 非同期バックグラウンドエージェントで作業を実行
 - 定期的にポーリングして作業内容を要約
 - 技術者ではない方向けに、簡潔で分かりやすく説明
 - 探索エージェントで仕組みを説明
 - エラー発生時はガイダンスを提供
 - 技術的な用語は使わない

※余談ですが、Claude in Chromeがあると、ポスト内容を表示させたまま文字起こし→翻訳が実行できて楽
